claim: Pain after surgery causes significant suffering.
source: Pain after surgery causes significant suffering.
evidence: This is a general statement about post-surgical pain that is part of established medical knowledge.

claim: Opioid analgesics cause severe side effects and accidental death.
source: Opioid analgesics cause severe side effects and accidental death.
evidence: This statement is supported by established medical knowledge and is referenced in the context of the opioid crisis.

claim: Local application of Clarix Flo (FLO) attenuated established post-surgical pain hypersensitivity without exhibiting known side effects of opioid use in mice.
source: Local application of Clarix Flo (FLO), a human amniotic membrane (AM) product, attenuated established post-surgical pain hypersensitivity without exhibiting known side effects of opioid use in mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including behavioral tests shown in Figure 1.

claim: FLO achieves pain inhibition through direct inhibition of nociceptive dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons via CD44-dependent pathways.
source: This effect was achieved through direct inhibition of nociceptive dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons via CD44-dependent pathways.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data including calcium imaging and electrophysiology studies, as well as experiments in CD44 knockout mice.

claim: HC-HA/PTX3 is the major matrix component purified from human AM that has greater purity and water solubility than FLO.
source: We further purified the major matrix component, the heavy chain-hyaluronic acid/pentraxin 3 (HC-HA/PTX3) from human AM that has greater purity and water solubility than FLO.
evidence: This claim is supported by the purification methods described and biochemical characterization shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: HC-HA/PTX3 replicated FLO-induced neuronal and pain inhibition.
source: HC-HA/PTX3 replicated FLO-induced neuronal and pain inhibition.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing similar effects of HC-HA/PTX3 and FLO in behavioral and electrophysiological studies.

claim: HC-HA/PTX3 induced cytoskeleton rearrangements to inhibit sodium current and high-voltage activated calcium current on nociceptive DRG neurons.
source: Mechanistically, HC-HA/PTX3-induced cytoskeleton rearrangements to inhibit sodium current and high-voltage activated calcium current on nociceptive DRG neurons, suggesting it is a key bioactive component mediating pain relief.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data including immunofluorescence studies of F-actin and patch-clamp recordings shown in Figure 5.

claim: Surgery or trauma may lead to persistent pain, impeding functional recovery and causing considerable distress.
source: Surgery or trauma may lead to persistent pain, impeding functional recovery and causing considerable distress (Kehlet et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Continuous reliance on opioid analgesics causes severe side effects and accidental death, which resulted in a national public health emergency being declared in 2017.
source: Continuous reliance on opioid analgesics causes severe side effects and accidental death, which resulted in a national public health emergency being declared in 2017 (Colvin et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature and references a known historical event.

claim: The birth tissue is predominantly comprised of the amniotic membrane (AM) and umbilical cord (UC), which share the same cell origin as the fetus.
source: The birth tissue is predominantly comprised of the amniotic membrane (AM) and umbilical cord (UC), which share the same cell origin as the fetus.
evidence: This is a statement based on established biological knowledge about fetal development.

claim: Birth tissues have been used as medical therapy in a wide range of conditions.
source: These versatile biological tissues have been used as medical therapy in a wide range of conditions (Chao et al., 1940; de Rotth, 1940).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: FLO is a sterile, micronized, and lyophilized form of human AM/UC matrix used for surgical and non-surgical repair, reconstruction, or replacement of soft tissue by filling in the connective tissue void.
source: FLO (Clarix Flo; BioTissue, Miami, FL) is a sterile, micronized, and lyophilized form of human AM/UC matrix used for surgical and non-surgical repair, reconstruction, or replacement of soft tissue by filling in the connective tissue void.
evidence: This is a description of the product based on manufacturer information and established knowledge about the product.

claim: FLO has been shown to orchestrate regenerative healing within its anti-inflammatory and anti-scarring properties in ophthalmic applications.
source: They have been shown to orchestrate regenerative healing within its anti-inflammatory and anti-scarring properties in ophthalmic applications (Tighe et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: FLO appears to relieve pain effectively in several ocular surface disorders.
source: Intriguingly, FLO also appears to relieve pain effectively in several ocular surface disorders (Espana et al., 2003; Finger, 2008; Morkin and Hamrah, 2018), and musculoskeletal disorders such as osteoarthritis (Castellanos and Tighe, 2019; Mead and Mead, 2020) and lower extremity neuropathy (Buksh, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: FLO appears to relieve pain effectively in musculoskeletal disorders such as osteoarthritis and lower extremity neuropathy.
source: Intriguingly, FLO also appears to relieve pain effectively in several ocular surface disorders (Espana et al., 2003; Finger, 2008; Morkin and Hamrah, 2018), and musculoskeletal disorders such as osteoarthritis (Castellanos and Tighe, 2019; Mead and Mead, 2020) and lower extremity neuropathy (Buksh, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The mechanisms underlying FLO's potential pain-inhibitory properties and how it may affect sensory neuron excitability remain unknown.
source: However, the mechanisms underlying its potential pain-inhibitory properties and how it may affect sensory neuron excitability remain unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: HC-HA/PTX3 was recently shown to alleviate dry eye disease induced by chronic graft-versus-host disease by suppressing inflammation and scarring in murine lacrimal glands.
source: HC-HA/PTX3 was recently shown to alleviate dry eye disease induced by chronic graft-versus-host disease by suppressing inflammation and scarring in murine lacrimal glands (Ogawa et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Intra-paw injection of FLO acutely inhibited heat nociception in naive wild-type (WT) mice.
source: Intra-paw injection of FLO, but not the vehicle (saline) acutely inhibited heat nociception in naive wild-type (WT) mice (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: FLO dose-dependently (0.1–0.5 mg) attenuated heat hypersensitivity in the hindpaw receiving the plantar-incision.
source: Moreover, FLO dose-dependently (0.1–0.5 mg) attenuated heat hypersensitivity in the hindpaw receiving the plantar-incision (Figure 1B), and inhibited mechanical hyperalgesia in the Randall–Sellito test (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: FLO inhibited mechanical hyperalgesia in the Randall–Sellito test.
source: Moreover, FLO dose-dependently (0.1–0.5 mg) attenuated heat hypersensitivity in the hindpaw receiving the plantar-incision (Figure 1B), and inhibited mechanical hyperalgesia in the Randall–Sellito test (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: FLO partially normalized the impaired gaiting caused by incision, as indicated by increases in print area and max contact area from pre-drug levels.
source: In the Catwalk assay, FLO partially normalized the impaired gaiting caused by incision, as indicated by increases in print area and max contact area from pre-drug levels (Figure 1D, E), suggesting an attenuation of movement-evoked pain which is common after surgery.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and 1E.

claim: FLO attenuates movement-evoked pain which is common after surgery.
source: In the Catwalk assay, FLO partially normalized the impaired gaiting caused by incision, as indicated by increases in print area and max contact area from pre-drug levels (Figure 1D, E), suggesting an attenuation of movement-evoked pain which is common after surgery.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the gait analysis data and the interpretation that improved gait parameters suggest reduced movement-evoked pain.

claim: FLO caused no impairment in locomotor function or exploratory activity in the open-field test.
source: FLO caused no impairment in locomotor function or exploratory activity in the open-field test (Figure 1F); these symptoms are known side effects of opioid use.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Impairment in locomotor function or exploratory activity are known side effects of opioid use.
source: FLO caused no impairment in locomotor function or exploratory activity in the open-field test (Figure 1F); these symptoms are known side effects of opioid use.
evidence: This is a statement based on established medical knowledge about opioid side effects.

claim: The concentration of FLO used fell within the range reported in previous clinical studies.
source: The concentration of FLO we used fell within the range reported in previous clinical studies (Ackley et al., 2019; Bennett, 2019; Castellanos and Tighe, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous clinical studies.

claim: Nociceptive neuron hyperexcitability may lead to persistent pain.
source: Since nociceptive neuron hyperexcitability may lead to persistent pain (Xie et al., 2005; Zimmermann, 2001), cellular mechanisms of pain inhibition by FLO can be partly inferred from its modulatory effects on these neurons' excitability.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Intra-paw injection of FLO selectively reduced the activation of small-diameter DRG neurons to noxious heat stimulation after plantar-incision.
source: Intra-paw injection of FLO selectively reduced the activation of small-diameter DRG neurons, which are mostly nociceptive neurons, to noxious heat stimulation after plantar-incision (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2B-D.

claim: Small-diameter DRG neurons are mostly nociceptive neurons.
source: Intra-paw injection of FLO selectively reduced the activation of small-diameter DRG neurons, which are mostly nociceptive neurons, to noxious heat stimulation after plantar-incision (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This is a statement based on established neuroscience knowledge about DRG neuron classification.

claim: Intra-paw injection of HC-HA/PTX3 dose-dependently (10–20 μg) induced heat antinociception in naive WT mice.
source: Like FLO, intra-paw injection of HC-HA/PTX3 dose-dependently (10–20 μg) induced heat antinociception in naive WT mice and attenuated heat hypersensitivity developed in the hindpaw after plantar-incision (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Intra-paw injection of HC-HA/PTX3 attenuated heat hypersensitivity developed in the hindpaw after plantar-incision.
source: Like FLO, intra-paw injection of HC-HA/PTX3 dose-dependently (10–20 μg) induced heat antinociception in naive WT mice and attenuated heat hypersensitivity developed in the hindpaw after plantar-incision (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: HC-HA/PTX3-induced pain inhibition was comparable between male and female mice after plantar-incision.
source: Moreover, HC-HA/PTX3-induced pain inhibition was comparable between male and female mice after plantar-incision (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: HMW-HA was suggested to attenuate inflammatory pain and neuropathic pain induced by the cancer chemotherapy paclitaxel.
source: HMW-HA, a major component of HC-HA/PTX3, was suggested to attenuate inflammatory pain and neuropathic pain induced by the cancer chemotherapy paclitaxel (Bonet et al., 2020; Bonet et al., 2021b; Bonet et al., 2022; Ferrari et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: HC-HA/PTX3 demonstrated a significantly more potent anti-hyperalgesic effect than HMW-HA at its peak (1 hr post-drug).
source: At its peak (1 hr post-drug), HC-HA/PTX3 demonstrated a significantly more potent anti-hyperalgesic effect than HMW-HA, and this effect persisted for over 4 hr (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The anti-hyperalgesic effect of HC-HA/PTX3 persisted for over 4 hr.
source: At its peak (1 hr post-drug), HC-HA/PTX3 demonstrated a significantly more potent anti-hyperalgesic effect than HMW-HA, and this effect persisted for over 4 hr (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The effect of HMW-HA had largely dissipated by approximately the 4 hr mark.
source: In contrast, the effect of HMW-HA had largely dissipated by approximately the 4 hr mark.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A mixture of HMW-HA and HC1 did not demonstrate a greater pain-inhibitory effect compared to HMW-HA alone.
source: However, this mixture did not demonstrate a greater pain-inhibitory effect compared to HMW-HA alone (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The full HC-HA/PTX3 complex is superior to HMW-HA in attenuating post-surgical pain.
source: These findings suggest that the full HC-HA/PTX3 complex is superior to HMW-HA in attenuating post-surgical pain.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparative experimental data showing HC-HA/PTX3 has greater efficacy than HMW-HA or HMW-HA+HC1.

claim: HC-HA/PTX3 significantly reduced the [Ca2+]i increase produced by capsaicin, cinnamaldehyde, and β-alanine in DRG neurons.
source: Here, HC-HA/PTX3 (15 μg/ml) significantly reduced the [Ca2+]i increase produced by these proalgesics.
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3C-F.

claim: HMW-HA (15 μg/ml) was not effective at reducing capsaicin-evoked calcium responses at the same concentration as HC-HA/PTX3.
source: However, HMW-HA (15 μg/ml) was not effective at the same concentration (Figure 3C–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3C-F.

claim: HC-HA/PTX3 concentration-dependently hyperpolarized the membrane potential in small DRG neurons.
source: In small DRG neurons, HC-HA/PTX3 concentration-dependently hyperpolarized the membrane potential (5, 10, and 25 μg/ml, Figure 3G, I), and increased the rheobase (Figure 3H, J), indicating decreased neuronal excitability.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3G and 3I.

claim: HC-HA/PTX3 increased the rheobase in small DRG neurons, indicating decreased neuronal excitability.
source: In small DRG neurons, HC-HA/PTX3 concentration-dependently hyperpolarized the membrane potential (5, 10, and 25 μg/ml, Figure 3G, I), and increased the rheobase (Figure 3H, J), indicating decreased neuronal excitability.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3H and 3J.

claim: HC-HA/PTX3 (10 μg/ml) did not significantly affect the intrinsic membrane excitability of large neurons.
source: However, HC-HA/PTX3 (10 μg/ml) did not significantly affect the IME of large neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: HC-HA/PTX3 may attenuate the activation of key receptors involved in pain control such as TRPV1, TRPA1, and MrgprD.
source: These findings suggest that HC-HA/PTX3 may attenuate the activation of key receptors involved in pain control such as TRPV1, TRPA1, and MrgprD.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the calcium imaging data showing reduced responses to agonists of these receptors.

claim: HC-HA/PTX3 fundamentally decreases nociceptor excitability by inducing membrane hyperpolarization and altering intrinsic membrane properties.
source: Additionally, it fundamentally decreases nociceptor excitability by inducing membrane hyperpolarization and altering intrinsic membrane properties.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data showing changes in membrane potential and rheobase.

claim: CD44 is a multifunctional transmembrane glycoprotein that functions as a cell surface adhesion receptor, regulating essential physiologic and pathologic processes.
source: CD44 is a multifunctional transmembrane glycoprotein that functions as a cell surface adhesion receptor, regulating essential physiologic and pathologic processes (Campo et al., 2010; Janiszewska et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CD44 is the principal receptor for HA.
source: CD44 is the principal receptor for HA (Ferrari et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: CD44 is expressed in both neurons and glial cells.
source: CD44 is expressed in both neurons and glial cells (Dzwonek and Wilczynski, 2015), but its distribution in the DRG was unclear.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In mouse DRG, CD44 immuno-reactivity highly colocalized with Na-K ATPase alpha1, a neuron surface marker.
source: In mouse DRG, CD44 immuno-reactivity highly colocalized with Na-K ATPase alpha1, a neuron surface marker, but presented at a much lower level in satellite glial cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CD44 immuno-reactivity presented at a much lower level in satellite glial cells compared to neurons.
source: In mouse DRG, CD44 immuno-reactivity highly colocalized with Na-K ATPase alpha1, a neuron surface marker, but presented at a much lower level in satellite glial cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CD44 immuno-reactivity highly colocalized with CGRP and IB4, markers of small peptidergic and non-peptidergic nociceptive DRG neurons.
source: CD44 immuno-reactivity highly colocalized with CGRP and IB4, markers of small peptidergic and non-peptidergic nociceptive DRG neurons (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) dataset of mouse DRG showed high expression levels of CD44 in nociceptive neuronal clusters.
source: Consistent with this finding, analysis of our recently published single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) dataset of mouse DRG showed high expression levels of CD44 in nociceptive neuronal clusters (Figure 4B; Zhang et al., 2022), but much lower expression in large neuronal clusters which are Aβ or Aδ low-threshold mechanoreceptors or proprioceptors, and in C-fiber low-threshold mechanoreceptors (c-LTMRs, Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4B and cited from a previous publication.

claim: CD44 expression is much lower in large neuronal clusters which are Aβ or Aδ low-threshold mechanoreceptors or proprioceptors, and in C-fiber low-threshold mechanoreceptors.
source: Consistent with this finding, analysis of our recently published single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) dataset of mouse DRG showed high expression levels of CD44 in nociceptive neuronal clusters (Figure 4B; Zhang et al., 2022), but much lower expression in large neuronal clusters which are Aβ or Aδ low-threshold mechanoreceptors or proprioceptors, and in C-fiber low-threshold mechanoreceptors (c-LTMRs, Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: HC-HA/PTX3 did not reduce the capsaicin-evoked increase of [Ca2+]i in cultured lumbar DRG neurons from CD44 KO mice.
source: Importantly, in cultured lumbar DRG neurons from CD44 KO mice, HC-HA/PTX3 did not reduce the capsaicin-evoked increase of [Ca2+]i (Figure 4C–E), nor did it alter the IME and the membrane potential (Figure 4F, G).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4C-E.

claim: HC-HA/PTX3 did not alter the intrinsic membrane excitability and the membrane potential in DRG neurons from CD44 KO mice.
source: Importantly, in cultured lumbar DRG neurons from CD44 KO mice, HC-HA/PTX3 did not reduce the capsaicin-evoked increase of [Ca2+]i (Figure 4C–E), nor did it alter the IME and the membrane potential (Figure 4F, G).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4F and 4G.

claim: The inhibition of heat hyperalgesia by FLO was diminished in CD44 KO mice.
source: Behaviorally, the inhibition of heat hyperalgesia by FLO (0.5 mg, 20 μl) and by HC-HA/PTX3 (10 or 20 μg, 20 μl) was both diminished in CD44 KO mice (Figure 4H, I).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The inhibition of heat hyperalgesia by HC-HA/PTX3 was diminished in CD44 KO mice.
source: Behaviorally, the inhibition of heat hyperalgesia by FLO (0.5 mg, 20 μl) and by HC-HA/PTX3 (10 or 20 μg, 20 μl) was both diminished in CD44 KO mice (Figure 4H, I).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Applying a neutralizing antibody (IgG, 10 μg) to CD44 blocked HC-HA/PTX3-induced pain inhibition in WT mice.
source: Likewise, applying a neutralizing antibody (IgG, 10 μg) to CD44, but not control IgG blocked HC-HA/PTX3-induced pain inhibition in WT mice (Figure 4J).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: Pain inhibition by HC-HA/PTX3 and FLO is CD44-dependent.
source: Collectively, these findings suggest that pain inhibition, as well as the exclusive inhibition of small DRG neurons, which are mostly nociceptive, by HC-HA/PTX3 and FLO, are CD44-dependent.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined data showing loss of effect in CD44 KO mice and with CD44 neutralizing antibody.

claim: The exclusive inhibition of small DRG neurons by HC-HA/PTX3 and FLO is CD44-dependent.
source: Collectively, these findings suggest that pain inhibition, as well as the exclusive inhibition of small DRG neurons, which are mostly nociceptive, by HC-HA/PTX3 and FLO, are CD44-dependent.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined data showing loss of effect in CD44 KO mice and with CD44 neutralizing antibody.

claim: CD44 signaling plays a vital role in regulating the cytoskeleton, forming an intricate fibrous subcellular network that undergoes dynamic changes to regulate cell function.
source: CD44 signaling plays a vital role in regulating the cytoskeleton, forming an intricate fibrous subcellular network that undergoes dynamic changes to regulate cell function (Föger et al., 2001; Freeman et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: HC-HA/PTX3 (10, 15 μg/ml) significantly increased the translocation of F-actin to cell membranes in neurons from lumbar DRG of WT mice.
source: Immunofluorescence staining showed that HC-HA/PTX3 (10, 15 μg/ml) significantly increased the translocation of F-actin to cell membranes in neurons from lumbar DRG of WT mice (Figure 5A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: F-actin fibers were mostly retained in the cytoplasm in HMW-HA-treated (15 μg/ml) group.
source: However, F-actin fibers were mostly retained in the cytoplasm in HMW-HA-treated (15 μg/ml) group.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: HC-HA/PTX3 at the concentration (0–15 μg/ml) tested did not induce neuronal toxicity, per the MTT assay.
source: HC-HA/PTX3 at the concentration (0–15 μg/ml) tested did not induce neuronal toxicity, per the MTT (3-(4,5-dimethylthiazol-2-yl)-2,5-diphenyltetrazolium bromide) assay (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by MTT assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Pretreatment with CD44 IgG (2 µg/ml) blocked the cytoskeletal rearrangement induced by HC-HA/PTX3 (15 μg/ml).
source: Notably, pretreatment with CD44 IgG (2 µg/ml) blocked the cytoskeletal rearrangement induced by HC-HA/PTX3 (15 μg/ml, Figure 5E, F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5E and 5F.

claim: The condensation of sub-membranous F-actin and translocation of CD44 to the cell membrane after HC-HA/PTX3 were significantly increased only in small DRG neurons.
source: In line with this finding, the condensation of sub-membranous F-actin and translocation of CD44 to the cell membrane after HC-HA/PTX3 were significantly increased only in small DRG neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), which express much higher levels of CD44 than large neurons (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: CD44 may activate cytoskeletal proteins, such as Ank2-encoded Ankyrin-B and Ank3-encoded Ankyrin-G, which are highly expressed in DRG neurons and can modulate neuronal excitability.
source: CD44 may activate cytoskeletal proteins, such as Ank2-encoded Ankyrin-B and Ank3-encoded Ankyrin-G, which are highly expressed in DRG neurons and can modulate neuronal excitability (Stevens and Rasband, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: CD44 can interact with cortical actin filaments via ezrin/radixin/moesin (ERM) signaling.
source: CD44 can also interact with cortical actin filaments via ezrin/radixin/moesin (ERM) signaling (Fehon et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Both Ankyrin and ERM signaling may partly contribute to HC-HA/PTX3-induced cytoskeletal rearrangement.
source: Although HC-HA-PTX3 still increased the translocation of F-actin and CD44 to the cell membrane in both siAnk and siERM groups, the extent was significantly less than that in the siNT control group (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, B), suggesting that both Ankyrin and ERM signaling may partly contribute to HC-HA/PTX3-induced cytoskeletal rearrangement.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the siRNA knockdown experiments showing partial reduction of HC-HA/PTX3 effects.

claim: F-actin constitutes a sub-membranous cytoskeleton network, serving as an important scaffold for membrane ion channels, receptors, and intracellular kinases to function properly.
source: F-actin constitutes a sub-membranous cytoskeleton network, serving as an important scaffold for membrane ion channels, receptors, and intracellular kinases to function properly (Vasilev et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: HC-HA/PTX3 (10 µg/ml) inhibited depolarization-elicited INav in small neurons from the lumbar DRG in WT mice at Days 2–4 after plantar-incision.
source: HC-HA/PTX3 (10 µg/ml) inhibited depolarization-elicited INav in small neurons from the lumbar DRG in WT mice at Days 2–4 after plantar-incision, compared to the vehicle (Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: HC-HA/PTX3 treatment increased INav in DRG neurons from CD44 KO mice.
source: In contrast, the same treatment increased INav in that of CD44 KO mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A and 3B.

claim: Pretreatment with an intracellular infusion of LAT-A (0.5 nM) abolished the inhibition of INav by HC-HA/PTX3 in WT mice.
source: Importantly, pretreatment with an intracellular infusion of LAT-A (0.5 nM) abolished the inhibition of INav by HC-HA/PTX3 in WT mice; instead, an increased INav was observed (Figure 5G, Figure 5—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 3B.

claim: HC-HA/PTX3 inhibited the HVA-Ica current in WT DRG neurons.
source: HC-HA/PTX3 also inhibited the HVA-Ica current in WT DRG neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The inhibition of HVA-Ica by HC-HA/PTX3 was attenuated by intracellular infusion of LAT-A.
source: This effect was also attenuated by intracellular infusion of LAT-A (Figure 5H, Figure 5—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5H and Figure 5—figure supplement 3C.

claim: HC-HA/PTX3 may inhibit cell membrane ion channels through a CD44-mediated cytoskeleton rearrangement.
source: Collectively, these findings suggest that HC-HA/PTX3 may inhibit cell membrane ion channels through a CD44-mediated cytoskeleton rearrangement.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined data showing CD44-dependence and cytoskeleton-dependence of ion channel inhibition.

claim: Neither bath application of HC-HA/PTX3 (15 μg/ml) nor intracellular infusion of LAT-A (0.5 nM) changed the gross morphology of DRG neurons.
source: Despite the cytoskeletal effects, neither bath application of HC-HA/PTX3 (15 μg/ml) nor intracellular infusion of LAT-A (0.5 nM) changed the gross morphology of DRG neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy images shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: Human birth tissue products (FLO) mitigated post-surgical pain by directly inhibiting nociceptive DRG neurons.
source: Our study revealed that human birth tissue products (FLO) mitigated post-surgical pain by directly inhibiting nociceptive DRG neurons.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the combined experimental data from behavioral and neuronal studies.

claim: The major matrix component purified from human AM, HC-HA/PTX3, mimics the pain- and neuronal-inhibitory effects of FLO.
source: The major matrix component purified from human AM, HC-HA/PTX3, mimics the pain- and neuronal-inhibitory effects of FLO.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the comparative experimental data showing similar effects of FLO and HC-HA/PTX3.

claim: Both FLO and HC-HA/PTX3 exert pain inhibition in a CD44-dependent manner.
source: Mechanistically, both compounds exert pain inhibition in a CD44-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the experimental data in CD44 KO mice and with CD44 neutralizing antibody.

claim: HC-HA/PTX3 caused membrane hyperpolarization, modified the intrinsic properties, and inhibited INav and HVA-Ica in nociceptive DRG neurons through cytoskeleton rearrangement and interaction with these membrane ion channels.
source: At the cellular level, HC-HA/PTX3 caused membrane hyperpolarization, modified the intrinsic properties, and inhibited INav and HVA-Ica in nociceptive DRG neurons through cytoskeleton rearrangement and interaction with these membrane ion channels.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the combined electrophysiology and immunofluorescence data.

claim: Cryopreserved AM/UC has been clinically validated through numerous studies since 1995, including clinical trials specifically assessing FLO.
source: Cryopreserved AM/UC has been clinically validated through numerous studies since 1995, including clinical trials specifically assessing FLO (Clarix Flo).
evidence: This claim is based on the historical record of clinical studies.

claim: Clinical studies collectively support the safety and preliminary effectiveness of FLO in managing some clinical pain conditions such as knee osteoarthritis, discogenic pain, rotator cuff tears, and painful neuropathy of the lower extremities.
source: These studies collectively support the safety and preliminary effectiveness of FLO in managing some clinical pain conditions such as knee osteoarthritis (Castellanos and Tighe, 2019; Mead and Mead, 2020), discogenic pain (Buck, 2019), rotator cuff tears (Ackley et al., 2019), and painful neuropathy of the lower extremities (Buksh, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous clinical studies.

claim: Treatment with HC-HA/PTX3 demonstrated a stronger and longer-lasting pain-inhibitory effect compared to treatment with HMW-HA and the combination of HMW-HA and HC1, at their comparable dosages tested.
source: Intriguingly, treatment with HC-HA/PTX3 demonstrated a stronger and longer-lasting pain-inhibitory effect compared to treatment with HMW-HA and the combination of HMW-HA and HC1, at their comparable dosages tested.

claim: HC-HA/PTX3, but not HMW-HA, induced a rearrangement of the cytoskeleton, leading to an increase in sub-membranous F-actin polymerization and the translocation of CD44 to the vicinity of the cell membrane in small DRG neurons.
source: To explore the molecular basis of HC-HA/PTX3-induced neuronal inhibition, our study unraveled that HC-HA/PTX3, but not HMW-HA, induced a rearrangement of the cytoskeleton, leading to an increase in sub-membranous F-actin polymerization and the translocation of CD44 to the vicinity of the cell membrane in small DRG neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The cytoskeletal rearrangement effect of HC-HA/PTX3 was not observed in large DRG neurons.
source: This effect was not observed in large DRG neurons, and was blocked by both LAT-A pretreatment and Pfn1 knockdown, which disrupt actin polymerization.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The cytoskeletal rearrangement effect of HC-HA/PTX3 was blocked by both LAT-A pretreatment and Pfn1 knockdown, which disrupt actin polymerization.

claim: Polymerized F-actin serves as a scaffold for signaling that affects ion channels.
source: Given that polymerized F-actin serves as a scaffold for signaling that affects ion channels, we speculate that the cytoskeleton rearrangement triggered by HC-HA/PTX3 could thus profoundly change ion channel function and, consequently, neuronal excitability.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about cytoskeleton function.
